newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Latest Sri Lanka attacks prove rebels' strike power.
newsitem.headline: Latest Sri Lanka attacks prove rebels' strike power.

text.p: The latest attacks on two Sri Lankan military bases by Tamil Tiger fighters merely reinforces the rebels' ability to strike at will and has little to do with recent military gains, diplomats and analysts said on Friday.
"It is part and parcel of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam's (LTTE) strategy to show they can exert armed pressure on the army," said political analyst Paikiasothy Saravanamuttu.

"It is the LTTE's way of saying 'Whatever anyone might say, we're still in the game and we can inflict damage whenever we want to,'" said Saravanamuttu, a consultant at the Centre for Policy Studies and Alternatives, an independent think-tank.

The Ministry of Defence said on Friday at least 200 rebels and 65 soldiers were killed when the rebels attacked a military camp at Vavunathivu near the eastern town of Batticaloa, about 200 km (125 miles) east of the capital Colombo.
Military officials said the camp was overrun by a group of more than 800 rebels in a pre-dawn attack. The camp was later retaken by government forces.

A small group of rebels and suicide bombers launched a simultaneous attack on China Bay air force base in eastern Trincomalee, some 240 km (150 miles) from Colombo, killing one airman and destroying a transport plane.

The attacks came after government forces last month captured a key highway linking two army-held towns in the north of the island with little opposition from the rebels, who previously controlled large areas to the south and the southwest of the highway.
"The LTTE are making a political as well as a military statement. They are saying 'We're still here and we still are key players,'" Saravanamuttu said.

Former air force chief Air Vice Marshall Harry Goonetileke said the attack on the well-defended China Bay base showed the LTTE's ability to sneak in small groups for surprising, fast attacks on selected targets.
"It showed the audacity of the LTTE. It was a mere sabotage call by the Tigers. And it was a typical trademark LTTE guerrilla attack," Goonetileke said.

The LTTE is fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in this predominantly Sinhalese island's north and east. The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the civil war, now in its 14th year, while the LTTE says the figure is higher.
Analysts said Thursday's attacks were not in retaliation for the highway's capture.
"I don't see it as being in retaliation for anything. The Tigers have carried out this sort of attack on camps before," said a Western diplomat.
Last year, the LTTE overran an important army base at Mullaitivu on the northeast coast, killing or capturing the camp's 1,000 men and dealing the the military its worst blow of the war.
In January, the rebels attacked a military base at Paranthan, a key road junction south of Jaffna. The army said 223 soldiers died and the rebels said they lost at least 140.

"The Tigers are going to carry out this sort of attack every now and then and some army camps are going to be more vulnerable than the others," the diplomat said. "It is a good way for them to show that they still are a strong military force."
